subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: According to Kepler's first law, what is the shape of a planet's orbit around the Sun?
questions.explain: Kepler's first law states that planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.

questions.q: In Kepler's first law, where is the Sun located within a planet's elliptical orbit?
options: At the exact centre of the ellipse
At one focus of the ellipse
At the edge of the ellipse
questions.explain: An ellipse has two foci, and Kepler's first law places the Sun at one of them.

questions.q: Kepler's second law says a line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. What does this imply about the planet's speed?
options: It moves fastest when closest to the Sun
It moves fastest when furthest from the Sun
It moves at a constant speed throughout
questions.explain: To sweep equal areas in equal times, a planet must travel faster near perihelion (closest approach) and slower near aphelion.

questions.q: Which relationship correctly expresses Kepler's third law, where T is orbital period and r is the mean orbital radius?
options: T squared is proportional to r cubed
T cubed is proportional to r squared
T is proportional to r squared
questions.explain: Kepler's third law states that the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the mean orbital radius.

questions.q: A planet orbits a star at 4 times the orbital radius of another planet around the same star. Using Kepler's third law (T squared proportional to r cubed), how many times longer is its orbital period?
questions.explain: T squared is proportional to r cubed, so if r increases 4 times, T squared increases 64 times and T increases 8 times.

questions.q: A comet on a highly elliptical orbit is observed to speed up as it approaches the Sun. Which of Kepler's laws best explains this behaviour?
questions.explain: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) requires faster motion near the Sun, so a comet speeds up at perihelion.

questions.q: Which equation represents Newton's law of gravitation for the force F between two masses m1 and m2 separated by distance r?
options: F = G m1 m2 / r squared
F = G m1 m2 r squared
questions.explain: Newton's law of gravitation gives the attractive force as F = G m1 m2 divided by the square of the separation.

questions.q: In Newton's law of gravitation, what does the symbol G represent?
questions.explain: G is the universal gravitational constant, the same value everywhere in the universe.

questions.q: Newton's law of gravitation is an inverse square law. If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force becomes:
questions.explain: Because force depends on 1 over r squared, doubling the distance reduces the force to one quarter.

questions.q: Two masses experience a gravitational force F. If the distance between them is tripled while the masses stay the same, the new force is:
questions.explain: Tripling the distance increases r squared by a factor of 9, so the force falls to F divided by 9.

questions.q: If one of the two masses in a gravitational interaction is doubled while the separation stays constant, the gravitational force between them:
questions.explain: Force is directly proportional to each mass, so doubling one mass doubles the force.

questions.q: The gravitational force described by Newton's law of gravitation is always:
questions.explain: Gravity is always an attractive force acting between any two masses.

questions.q: What is the orbital period of a satellite in a geostationary orbit?
questions.explain: A geostationary satellite orbits with a period of 24 hours, matching the Earth's rotation.

questions.q: What provides the centripetal force that keeps a satellite in a circular orbit around the Earth?
questions.explain: Gravitational attraction between the Earth and the satellite acts as the centripetal force keeping it in orbit.

questions.q: Satellites in a low polar orbit are especially useful for which of the following?
options: Live television broadcasting to a fixed dish
Imaging and monitoring the whole of the Earth's surface
Remaining fixed above one point on the equator
Communicating with a single ground station continuously
questions.explain: A polar-orbiting satellite passes over different regions as the Earth rotates beneath it, making it ideal for mapping and weather imaging.

questions.q: Why does a geostationary satellite appear to stay fixed above one point on the Earth?
options: It is not actually moving in space
Its orbital period equals the Earth's rotation period and it orbits above the equator
It orbits over the poles very quickly
It is held in place by the Earth's magnetic field
questions.explain: A geostationary satellite orbits over the equator with a 24 hour period, so it rotates in step with the Earth and appears stationary.

questions.q: Compared with the near-circular orbits of the planets, the orbit of a typical comet is:
questions.explain: Comets follow very elongated, highly eccentric elliptical orbits that bring them close to the Sun and then far away.

questions.q: Two satellites orbit the Earth. Using Kepler's third law, how does the orbital period of the satellite in a lower orbit compare with the one in a higher orbit?
options: The lower satellite has a shorter period
The lower satellite has a longer period
Both have exactly the same period
The lower satellite does not orbit at all
questions.explain: By Kepler's third law, a smaller orbital radius means a shorter orbital period, so lower satellites orbit faster.

questions.q: Two masses attract each other with force F. If both masses are doubled while the distance stays the same, the new gravitational force is:
questions.explain: Force is proportional to the product of the masses, so doubling each mass multiplies the force by 2 times 2, giving 4F.
